questions.question: Describe the production of a wheelie bin from recycled pellet and explain why injection moulding is only economical for large numbers.
questions.expected_answer: Recycled polypropylene pellet is blended with black masterbatch containing colour and UV stabiliser, dried and fed into an injection moulding machine, where a heated screw melts it and injects it under high pressure into a large two-part cooled steel mould; the melt is held under pressure while it cools for about a minute, the mould opens and the bin body is ejected. The lid and wheels are injection moulded on smaller machines, a steel axle is fitted, and the bin is assembled, stamped and stacked; runners and rejects are ground and fed back into the hopper. The mould costs millions of rand to make from hardened steel, so its cost must be spread over hundreds of thousands of parts, which makes injection moulding cheap per part only when the production run is very large.

questions.question: Describe injection moulding, blow moulding, extrusion and rotational moulding and give one product made by each.
questions.expected_answer: Injection moulding melts pellets with a heated screw and injects the melt under high pressure into a closed, cooled steel mould that opens and ejects a solid, detailed part such as a crate, cap or car bumper. Blow moulding clamps a tube of melt, the parison, in a mould and inflates it with air so it takes the shape of the mould, making hollow containers with a neck such as bottles, drums and jerry cans; PET bottles are stretch-blow moulded from a preform. Extrusion pushes melt continuously through a shaped die and cools it, making long products of constant cross-section such as pipe, gutter, cable sheath, window profile and film. Rotational moulding heats a hollow mould containing powdered plastic while rotating it on two axes so the powder melts and coats the inside evenly, making large seamless hollow items such as water tanks, canoes and road barriers.

questions.question: State the rules for designing a part to be injection moulded and explain the reason for each.
questions.expected_answer: Walls should be of even thickness, because thick sections shrink more and later than thin ones as they cool, causing sink marks, voids and warping; stiffness is gained with ribs instead. Walls parallel to the direction the mould opens need a draft angle, a taper of a degree or two, so the part can slide out of the mould. Undercuts, features that would lock the part in the mould, must be avoided or need costly moving mould parts. Inside corners are rounded, because sharp corners concentrate stress and hinder the flow of melt. The gate, where melt enters, leaves a mark and is placed where it will not show. A process is chosen to fit the shape and the number of parts, so injection moulding is not chosen for a run of a few parts, and thermosets are not injection moulded in this way because they do not melt.
